text.p: The following are the main stories from Tuesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- New banknotes should make forgery more difficult
- The search for a compromise has begun. Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition and the opposition Social Democrats started to find ways of agreeing on government's tax reform bill
- Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber says it would be better to delay European economic and monetary union (EMU) than to launch a weak euro
- Row over builders' pay agreement in Brandenburg, the state surrounding Berlin
- Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt sees potential for billions of marks of business in electronic data traffic at two-day technology conference in Bonn
HANDELSBLATT
- TV station ProSieben shares get off to a furious start, after being 50 times oversubscribed
- German Metro retail group seeks a new dimension
- Government ministers and industry representatives seek ways of establishing uniform rules for the Internet
- Price of gold falls further

- CDU/CSU deputy parliamentary group leader Rupert Scholz says complaints to the German Constitutional Court against Germany's participation in European economic and monetary union (EMU) will not succeed in derailing the project
- Hologram should make German banknotes more secure and more difficult to forge

- Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber and premier of Baden-Wuerttemberg regional state, Erwin Teufel, threaten to take case to German supreme court if their complaint about balancing budgets of regional states is not heeded.
- Metro retailing group also wants to create Cash and Carry giant store in Europe
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- The liberal Free Democrats fear Germany's reputation may have been damaged by scandal in which German soldiers staged mock executions and rapes and made videos of them

- Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt says there should be no new taxes on the Internet. He calls on international conference on technology for consensus between countries on data protection and criminal offences
- ProSieben shares rise by 32 percent on first day
DIE WELT

- Fresh row over the euro, taxes and solidarity tax surcharge, levied to help fund the reconstruction of former East Germany. Experts estimate Germany's budget deficit at 3.5 percent of gross domestic product. Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber wants delay if criteria are not exactly fulfilled.
- Turbulent start for ProSeiben shares. They rise from 72 to 95 marks on first day of trade. Banks recommend a quick sell
- German President Roman Herzog warns against the dangers of globalisation

- Germany as an industrial location for the telecommunications market is catching up. Germany is one of the most liberal markets in the world, according to Post Minister Wolfgang Boetsch addressing an international technology conference in Bonn
